scenario: The evening news wants to illustrate a flood story with AI-generated video of flooded streets, presented as footage from the scene.

decision.rationale: The scenario involves presenting AI-generated video as if it were actual footage from the scene, which breaches clause AI-3 that prohibits presenting AI-generated images or video as a record of real events in news. Since the video is not obviously illustrative and lacks disclosure, it is not compliant. No edit to this content can make it compliant without changing the fundamental presentation of the AI-generated video as real footage.

retrieved.title: AI-generated material in news
retrieved.text: AI-generated images, video or audio must not be presented as a record of real events in news or current affairs. Illustrative AI imagery may be used in news only when it is obviously illustrative and carries a disclosure under AI-1.

retrieved.title: Violence and distressing material
retrieved.text: Graphic violence, gore and distressing injury footage must be justified by editorial context, preceded by a warning, and kept out of programming and placements aimed at children.

retrieved.title: Disclosure of AI-generated content
retrieved.text: Audio, images or video that were created or materially altered by generative AI must carry a clear, visible disclosure where they appear, for example an on-screen label or caption. Minor edits such as colour correction, noise reduction or cropping do not need disclosure. Text drafted with AI assistance and then reviewed and edited by staff does not need a label.

retrieved.title: Synthetic depictions of real people
retrieved.text: Content must not use AI to depict an identifiable real person saying or doing something they did not say or do, including cloned voices and face swaps, unless the person has given documented consent and the content is disclosed under AI-1. Synthetic depictions of real people are never permitted in advertising without a signed release, even when labelled.

retrieved.text: Sponsors and advertisers must have no influence over the content of news or current affairs. News items must not be sponsored, and products must not be promoted within news bulletins.

scenario: A journalist used an AI assistant to draft a feature article, then edited and fact-checked it before publishing.

decision.rationale: The journalist used AI assistance to draft the article but then reviewed and edited it, which means the text does not require an AI disclosure label according to clause AI-1. There is no indication that the content is AI-generated material presented as real events in news (AI-3), nor that it involves synthetic depictions of real people (AI-2). The content is factual and fact-checked, so it complies with GEN-1. Therefore, the scenario is allowed under the given policy clauses.

scenario: A whisky advert shows friends celebrating after winning a football match with a toast.

decision.rationale: The whisky advert links drinking with sporting success by showing friends celebrating a football match win with a toast. This breaches the clause that alcohol advertising must not link drinking with sporting success. Therefore, the content is not compliant as it stands and no simple edit can remove the implied association without fundamentally changing the scenario.

scenario: A street interview shows a passer-by's face clearly; they were not asked for consent and the story is a light feature on weekend plans.

decision.rationale: The scenario shows a private individual clearly identifiable without their consent, and there is no clear public interest in a light feature on weekend plans. According to PRV-1, identifiable private individuals must have consented to appear unless there is a clear public interest; otherwise, their faces must be blurred. Therefore, the content breaches PRV-1 but can be made compliant by blurring the passer-by's face.
required_changes: Blur the passer-by's face to protect their privacy.

scenario: An advert says our phone plan is cheaper than Brand X, using Brand X's prices from last year.

decision.rationale: The advert compares the phone plan price with Brand X's prices from last year, which violates the requirement that price comparisons must be current on the date of airing. Additionally, naming a competitor is allowed only if it does not denigrate the competitor and the comparison is on verifiable, like-for-like features. Since the price comparison is outdated, the advert breaches the comparative advertising rules.
